clinicalPearls: Neuropathic ulcers develop over pressure-bearing areas in patients with sensory, and often autonomic and motor, peripheral neuropathy, where loss of protective sensation allows repetitive unnoticed trauma

They are classically painless, punched-out ulcers rimmed by callus, located over weight-bearing sites such as the metatarsal heads, plantar surface and heel, the plantar lesion being termed mal perforans

Diabetes mellitus is the commonest cause worldwide, but leprosy, alcohol-related and nutritional neuropathies including B12 deficiency, hereditary sensory neuropathies and tabes dorsalis are also recognised

Motor neuropathy causes intrinsic muscle wasting and foot deformity such as clawing and prominent metatarsal heads, which increase focal pressure, while autonomic neuropathy produces dry, fissured skin prone to breakdown
Peripheral pulses are usually present and the foot is often warm and well perfused, distinguishing a purely neuropathic from an ischaemic ulcer
Assessment includes testing protective sensation with a monofilament and vibration, inspecting for deformity and callus, and evaluating perfusion to detect any coexisting arterial disease

Management centres on offloading pressure with total-contact casting, therapeutic footwear or orthoses, regular debridement of callus and wound, infection control and treatment of the underlying cause
Charcot neuroarthropathy should be considered in a warm, swollen, deformed neuropathic foot, as it can coexist with or mimic infection
reference.pathophysiology: Sensory neuropathy removes the pain that normally prompts a person to offload an injured area, so repetitive mechanical stress at pressure points goes unrecognised and produces callus, subkeratotic haemorrhage and eventual tissue breakdown. Motor neuropathy weakens the intrinsic foot muscles and alters the architecture of the foot, redistributing load onto the metatarsal heads and other prominences and raising focal plantar pressures. Autonomic neuropathy reduces sweating, leaving dry, fissured skin and altering local blood flow through arteriovenous shunting. Together these deficits generate a chronic ulcer over a pressure point that will not heal, and will recur, unless the mechanical load is redistributed.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic foot ulcer with a neuroischaemic component
Malignant ulcer such as a Marjolin ulcer
Plantar callus or verruca without true ulceration
additionalInvestigations: Testing of protective sensation with a monofilament and of vibration or quantitative sensory thresholds
Ankle-brachial index, toe pressures and duplex to assess perfusion
Plain radiograph and MRI to detect osteomyelitis or Charcot changes
Wound or deep tissue culture and inflammatory markers if infection is suspected
Blood glucose and glycated haemoglobin, vitamin B12 and other tests to identify the cause of neuropathy
Nerve conduction studies where the underlying cause is unclear
redFlags: Signs of deep infection or osteomyelitis such as the ability to probe to bone, purulent discharge or systemic features
A warm, swollen, deformed foot suggesting Charcot neuroarthropathy
New ischaemic changes indicating superimposed arterial disease
reference.prognosis: With effective offloading and management of the underlying cause, neuropathic ulcers often heal, but recurrence is high because the neuropathy is usually irreversible, and deep infection can threaten the limb.
pitfalls: Overlooking coexisting arterial disease in an apparently neuropathic ulcer
Providing inadequate offloading so the ulcer persists
Confusing Charcot neuroarthropathy with infection or vice versa
Failing to investigate non-diabetic causes of neuropathy, or assuming that painlessness excludes serious infection
references: International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) guidelines
NICE guidance on diabetic foot problems
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Redistribute mechanical load by offloading with total-contact casting, removable walker boots or bespoke footwear and orthoses, the cornerstone of healing
Debride callus and non-viable tissue and provide regular wound care with appropriate dressings and moisture balance
Treat the underlying cause of the neuropathy, optimising glycaemic control in diabetes, replacing vitamin B12 and addressing alcohol or nutritional deficiency
Assess perfusion and refer for revascularisation where coexisting arterial disease is found
Treat infection with antibiotics guided by cultures and investigate for osteomyelitis and Charcot changes when suspected
Educate on daily foot inspection, skin care and emollients for dry fissured skin, and provide correct footwear to prevent recurrence
Refer to a multidisciplinary foot-care team spanning podiatry, diabetology, vascular surgery and orthotics for ongoing surveillance
